text:
Keep the Pen Moving: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years someone proposes that joined-up handwriting should go the way of the slide rule. Children type, the argument runs; adults type; exams are moving on screen; and the hours spent coaxing seven-year-olds to loop an "f" into an "l" could go to coding, or reading, or simply more maths. Finland dropped its cursive requirement in 2016. The American Common Core standards of 2010 left cursive out altogether. The case for abolition sounds modern and unsentimental.

I think it is wrong. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. My reason is not that it is beautiful or traditional, though it can be both. It is that fluent handwriting is still a working tool for thinking and learning, that joining is the most reliable route to fluency, and that the cost of teaching it is small beside the cost of leaving children without it.

Start with what handwriting does for a child who is learning to read and write. Forming a letter by hand is not the same act as pressing a key. A key press is identical for every letter; the finger does the same thing whether it produces a "b" or a "d". Drawing the letter requires the child to build it stroke by stroke, and that motor act appears to help fix the letter's shape in memory. Brain-imaging work by Karin James and colleagues found that pre-literate children who had practised writing letters by hand showed activity in reading-related regions when they later saw those letters, while children who had typed or traced them did not show the same pattern. EEG studies from Audrey van der Meer's lab in Norway have reported richer patterns of brain connectivity during handwriting than during typing. None of these studies is the last word, and brain activity is not the same as learning, but they point in one direction and they fit what teachers of early reading have long observed: writing letters helps children know letters.

The second argument concerns composition. Writing is hard for children because it makes several demands at once. They must decide what to say, find the words, spell them, and get the marks onto the page. Working memory is limited, and whatever is not automatic competes for it. Virginia Berninger's research over several decades showed that handwriting fluency in the primary years predicts both the amount and the quality of what children write, and that teaching handwriting explicitly improves composition, not just neatness. A child who must stop and think about how to form each letter has less attention left for the sentence. A child whose hand runs on its own can think about the story.

This is where joining earns its place. The honest position is that the evidence for cursive specifically, as against a well-taught print script, is thinner than its enthusiasts claim. Studies comparing the two are few and their results are mixed. What the evidence supports firmly is fluency. But joining is a method for producing fluency. A joined hand keeps the pen on the paper, cuts out the lifts and repositionings between letters, and makes the word, not the letter, the unit of movement. Children who learn a simple, sensible joined script generally write faster once it is secure, and speed matters in a way that is easy to underrate: a child who cannot keep up with their own thoughts loses them. Joining also gives each word a physical shape and rhythm, which many teachers find helps spelling, since common letter strings such as "ing" or "tion" become single practised movements. And for some children who reverse letters or leave ragged gaps in printed words, a continuous script removes the opportunity for the error.

Opponents reply that all of this could be achieved with a keyboard. Type fast enough, they say, and transcription stops competing with thought just as it does for a fluent writer. That is true for adults and older students who touch-type well. It is not true for six-year-olds. Small hands on a full-size keyboard, hunting for letters arranged in no logical order, are slower than the same hands with a pencil, and touch typing is itself a skill that takes sustained teaching, which few primary schools provide. The realistic alternative to teaching handwriting well is not a class of fluent typists. It is a class of children who are slow at both.

Nor does the adult world make handwriting obsolete as completely as the abolitionists assume. Most public examinations in Britain are still written by hand, for hours at a time, and will be for years yet; a child sent to secondary school with a slow, cramped print is at a real disadvantage at sixteen. Outside examinations, people still annotate, sketch out ideas, label, fill in forms, write cards, and take notes in settings where a laptop is unwelcome or a distraction. The well-known study by Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer, which found that students taking longhand notes understood lectures better than those typing, has not replicated cleanly, and I would not rest the case on it. But the mechanism it proposed is plausible and familiar to anyone who has done both: the typist can transcribe verbatim without thinking, while the hand writer, being slower, has to select and summarise. A tool that forces some processing is worth keeping in the kit.

There is a further point about access. Handwriting needs a pencil and paper. It needs no battery, no login, no licence, and no household broadband. Schools that shift early writing onto devices tie a foundational skill to equipment that is unevenly distributed and frequently broken. The child from a home with no quiet laptop can still practise writing at the kitchen table. A curriculum should be cautious about making the basics depend on kit.

What of the opportunity cost? This is the strongest objection, and it deserves a straight answer. Curriculum time is finite and every hour has rivals. But handwriting, taught properly, is cheap. The research on effective instruction points to short, frequent sessions, something like ten or fifteen minutes several times a week in the early years, tapering off once the script is automatic. That is a modest investment, and it pays back in every other subject, because every other subject requires children to write. The expensive version of handwriting teaching is the bad one: years of copying out in an ornate style, with endless correction of flourishes, long after the child can write legibly. The answer to that is a plain script and a clear end point, not abolition.

A related objection is that joined-up writing is cruel to children with dyspraxia, dysgraphia or other motor difficulties, who struggle with it and are made miserable. Some do, and for them a keyboard is a liberation that schools should offer early and without stigma. But a default is not a mandate without exceptions. We teach all children to read while making provision for those with dyslexia; we do not conclude that reading should be optional. It is also worth noting that some specialist teachers of children with dyslexia prefer a continuous joined script from the start, on the grounds that every letter begins in the same place and the word flows as a unit. The picture is more varied than "joining hurts the strugglers".

The experience of places that dropped cursive is instructive. In the United States, after the Common Core omitted it, a long list of states legislated it back into their classrooms; California's requirement took effect in 2024. Part of that was nostalgia, and part was the complaint that young people could not read their grandparents' letters or historical documents, which is a real loss but not a decisive one. Part of it, though, was the judgement of teachers and parents that something useful had been removed and nothing better had filled the space. England, meanwhile, has kept joined handwriting in its national curriculum throughout, and I see no evidence that its children are worse prepared for a digital world as a result.

That last point matters, because the debate is often framed as a choice between the pen and the keyboard. It is not. Children should learn to type, properly, and probably earlier and more systematically than most now do. The question is only whether, in the first years of school, they should also acquire a fast, legible, automatic hand. Given what handwriting contributes to learning letters, to spelling, and to freeing attention for composition, and given how little time it takes when taught well, the answer is yes.

So keep the handwriting lesson, and reform it. Teach a simple joined script without loops for loops' sake. Teach it in short daily bursts, early, and stop when it is secure. Judge it by speed and legibility, not by uniformity. Give keyboards to the children who need them and typing lessons to everyone. What we should not do is decide, on the strength of a hunch about the future, that a cheap skill with good evidence behind it is beneath a modern school.
